doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Woody Herman and the war years
title: USO work and a near assignment to South America
summary: In Abe Lyman's band he did USO shows; he was nearly sent as a quasi-spy musician to a neutral South American country.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well Woody Herman was 1944. Did you have to join the service?

Yeah that was before I was with Abe Lyman, And in Abe Lyman’s band we got in the USO. And at that time, I don’t know if the war was coming down, but Glenn Miller, his band got shot up or something, and we were all — I was a Captain. I mean you know, like a captain rating it was. And I had all my shots, and everyday we’d play different embarkation camps around, all over Jersey, they’d fly us up to New England, and we’d play a show, but we never knew if we were going with them or not. They wouldn’t tell you. You just said goodbye and you didn’t know. And then the bus would bring you back. And the next day they’d say we’re going to meet here. And that’s because you couldn’t talk you know.
They never told you where you were going?
No. They never told you. You were ready to go overseas. You were all ready to go. Because —
What was the phrase: loose lips sink ships? Something like that. So they didn’t want you to talk about where you were going.

Yeah, that’s right, that’s right. So I said goodbye so many times. Then they screened all the people in my neighborhood. I didn’t know this at the time then but the people started to tell my wife, they said, because they were going to send me to South America. They found out jazz was like the German Navy and the Italian Navy and the French Navy. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
They were down around South America. That was — what do you call it — a country not at war.

Yeah, a neutral country. So they found out they were going in to hear jazz. So they shipped some jazz bands in these little night clubs. So I was pegged to go down in there, in case it was — for a year, they called it you were the year. They sent me down and told me the job paid a hundred dollars a week. If you get killed, nobody knows anything about you. Your family gets nothing. They’re telling me, this is it. The Army — you’re not in the Army, you’re a spy. All you had to do was play, and if you were sitting like with the Germans or the Italians or something, and they said well we won’t see you for a while you know. And then every week or so you’d go to the embassy and say well this guy says he won’t be around for a while, while they were putting it together, that they were shipping out, all that kind of thing.
They wanted you to just give them information about—
But nobody knew anything about this. They didn’t want it. Because it was what kind of a country?

A neutral country. They didn’t want to say that they were behind it you know. And then in the USO, it was a hundred dollars a week too, but nothing else. And if anybody, if you were in battle, you weren’t shooting, but if you were in battle, your job, besides playing, was to pick up all the wounded or the dead. That was it. I mean you had to do that. I’m glad they didn’t shoot me.
